Author: @CurmudgeonExtraordinaire
Content:
I remember these back in school in the 1960s... When my daughter was in high school, I decided to visit it for lunch one day... Best I could tell, they don't actually cook anything from scratch anymore.  Everything comes from Sysco or wherever and they just reheat it... I toured their cafeteria at an "open house" event one evening and I was not impressed at all.  Nearly all of their cooking equipment was just for reheating things...

I had a taste for a sloppy joe about 20 years ago, so I did a bit of searching to find a recipe.  The recipe I found had meat, onion, bell pepper, ketchup, tomato paste, BBQ sauce, sugar, and Worcestershire sauce (and then seasoned to taste)... I replaced the bell pepper with a few jalapenos and added some finely chopped habanero peppers and crushed red peppers... Instead of adding water, I just take the last couple of ketchup and mustard bottles and put a bit of water in them to get the last dregs out of the bottles so I can finally toss them to be recycled...

The east bay city I was born in here in California also has a tradition of serving a sandwich called the "Pittsburger" named after my city Pittsburg, since the 1950s. Which is essentially sloppy joe meat, with some cheese (i never figured out what type) but with a very unique bun, its a square cut type of bread. The reason was they would make the bread from scratch back then so big flat rectangle loafs were easy to cut and served more kids. An article i'm reading calls it a lasagna sandwich so I guess thats what they were going for. Still the meat is very much sloppy joe style so it's fascinating how the sandwich itself evolved and became localized here into its own thing. 
Today even some local restaurants here have a "pittsburger" menu item and its exactly what you ate in school.

I'm a baby boomer and I remember we had sloppy joes in the cafeteria when I went to high school that would have been around 1966 through 69. Her high school was small and since it was in Michigan it was completely enclosed we always knew when it was sloppy Joe day because you could smell them all over the school. Sloppy joes and pizzas which ours were little round pizza for the two absolute favorite meals at the cafeteria. We had three women who look like they were somebody's grannies and they probably were who did all the cooking everything they made was from scratch and it was all delicious. The sloppy joes were still a favorite of school kids decades later when my daughter went to to a middle school. 

I remember making these from scratch one time as my daughter absolutely loves sloppy joes and usually it's the manwich ones that she likes. I think schools started ordering the manwich style sauce already made up ahead of time. The one time I made the sauce from scratch. my daughter was like.  Dad these are so good what did you put in them. It definitely makes a difference when you make the sauce yourself. And I agree the cheaper the bun the better the sloppy joe tastes. So now I have to make these again next time my daughter comes over to visit. Cuz even though she's a college student now she still loves her some sloppy joe.  Sometimes I use hamburger meat and a package of taco seasoning and I mix it and then I make sloppy joes with the taco meat filling some shredded lettuce and some shredded cheese just like you would if it was a taco on a bun. Some of your older followers like me will remember when Taco Bell made the Bell Beefer.  So nowadays I just make my own if I get the urge for one.

Author: @alanhyt79
Content:
I went to school in the 60s and 70s, kindergarten through HS graduation. My parents insisted that I bring a lunch instead of buying one. Normally, in the cafeteria where we all ate lunch, that was cool. School lunch usually looked pretty bad. But once in a while, they had Sloppy Joes. Such a heavenly scent filled the cafeteria on those days! One day, a classmate was complaining about "sloppy joes AGAIN??!" I traded him my pb & blackberry j sandwich for his sloppy joe. 
That is one of my most powerful memories from the late 60s and early 70s, that thing of perfection, the most scrumptious sandwich of my childhood. 
You say "80s and 90s"? What? Dude, just ask an older person about it, maybe bounce ideas off us oldsters, once in a while.
I saved my allowance so I could buy school lunch on sloppy joe days! Manwich is not the same. Was trying to give my kids the sloppy joe experience in the 80s and 90s, but the commercial product failed to bring back those memories of childhood culinary heaven. 
The recipe you quoted may have been from a later book, but those true, pure, real school sloppy joes came well before then. Your source is not the true origin of the recipe, brother. My favorite childhood food says otherwise.

Author: @WayneBarroncffcs
Content:
If you have a vacuum sealer.
Make double what he shows here.
Cook it up.
Cut up several portioned bags (make sure you double seal the bag at the bottom. This will help to ensure it does not leak in the freezer)
Fill with prepared sloppy Joe.
Seal and freeze.

This will make it easier to make in the future.
The warm-up.

Being a Pot of water to a boil.
Place the thawed-out bag in the pot and let it boil until thoroughly heated.

Doing it this way instead of in the microwave will help keep it moist, as I've noticed with other sealed meals, the microwave does work, but does not taste as good as it does when heated up in boiling water.

Author: @FireWireHTH
Content: We absolutely know what the sloppy joe sandwich from Cuba was like because all across NJ they still eat it. Its essentially their state sandwich. Its nothing like the sloppy joe the rest of everyone calls from school lunches. Its actual multiple types of cold cuts between multiple slices of very thin slices of rye bread with coleslaw and Russian dressing on top with the crust cut off,making for an extremely sloppy and messy eat. It came state side from Cuba with a NJ mayor who fell in love with the sandwich at you guessed it, Sloppy Joes in Cuba. He managed to convince the chef for the recipe that he brought home and asked a local deli to make him. That deli still makes them today and claims to be the Original NJ Sloppy Joe (Town Hall Deli). This sandwich actually predates what everyone else is calling the Sloppy Joe by a decade as it came to be in the late 1920's early 1930's and has become a sandwich you can now get everywhere in NJ. If i jad to guess, nobody created the sloppy joe we all loved as kids. It was created in a gov test kitchen to conserve tax dollars using ingredients they got cheaply at the time to make something that would resonate with kids so they wouldn't fuss and would just eat it. Needless to say clearly it worked because i don't know anyone from that time who didn't absolutely love sloppy joe's.

Author: @natfoote4967
Content: The name is likely an organic product of contemporary culture rather than the product of a single event. During the Great Depression, the urge for umami was often satisfied with cheap ground meat stretched out by other ingredients. When my mom worked in a drive-in theatre at that time she said they would put ground up green beans in the chili to stretch the sparsity of meat, because it had a similar texture to meat. Sloppy Joes are similar. It is a way to stretch one pound of cheap ground meat to feed a large family. The “sloppy” part of loose meat sandwiches is obvious. They are sloppy. The appeal of the “Joe” part very likely comes from that name signifying the common man. You see this in the term “GI Joe” and in Bill Mauldin’s “Willie and Joe” and in the Clint Eastwood “man with no name” character from the spaghetti westerns being called “Joe” at times. It is the generic name in the USA. So this is a cheap sandwich for an average ‘Joe’ who has a hankering for something meaty.

Author: @DirtyFrigginHarry
Content:
I've been working on elevating my sloppy joe game to luxurious comfort food status. It's become a nearly weekly meal. The key take aways I've had: 

1:  grill the bun. The crispy,  moderately browned layer of bread on the inside aids in the sandwich's integrity and more importantly provides textural crunch to a normally very flaccid albeit tasty meal.

2: make your own sauce, or at least doctor up the canned stuff. Fish sauce, rice vinegar, mustard seed, dehydrated onion, smoked paprika, gochujang, and beef broth have all become essentials for mine in addition to the standard tomato puree, worcestershire,  and sugar mixture. Red Pepper flakes or your favored hot sauce if you like it hot.

3: Ground pork and beef or just ground pork with added bacon or duck fat has become my go to meat, with a bit of cornstarch as needed for excess grease.

4: select and thoughtful toppings. A thin film of seasoned or plain mayo or aioli on the top and bottom bun adds a decadent and creamy richness. french fried jalapenos add crunch and heat. Sliced scallion greens and thinly shredded sharp cheddar are nice accents.

Author: @Malkmusianful
Content:
I'd love to see your take on the ground steak sandwich. Well, you and B. Dylan Hollis.

What is a ground steak? Well, it's a hyper-regional loose meat sandwich endemic to North Carolina, in particular Surry County and Yadkin County (iirc), that resembles a sloppy Joe but with a country gravy-like liquid binder and peppercorn instead of the tomato paste and onion used in the traditional sloppy Joe. It's only served in three counties - Surry, Yadkin, and the neighboring Virginia county of Carroll - and it doesn't get a lot of love on a national level. It doesn't look appetizing - the ground steak looks like if somebody mixed up Maid-Rite beef into a vat of country gravy - but it tastes amazing. It is the sort of food that I'd love to see given a spotlight - especially on Tasting History, where there's a treasure trove of 1900s recipes waiting to be discovered. And it'd be a great collaboration with B. Dylan Hollis since it's the type of hyper-regional food you'd only encounter on a meandering road trip.

Author: @symphoricquoz
Content:
Australian fellow, fairly comprehensive memory of the times, was once a secondary school student (like high school but 2), enjoys writing, so bear with; we had a cafeteria-lite space, basically an undercover (like, a fabric overhang) area with a sparse few tables, and a counter over which lunchstuffs flowed. The fare there that I remember getting included potato cakes, dim sims, slices such as caramel and hedgehog (the coconut thing, I don't think we hunt hedgehogs for meat here), and crumbed chicken rolls. I don't think they had soft drinks, since we had vending machines.
I think it was all much like that, the stuff that I don't remember, but we definitely didn't have any form of Joe or that style of meal. It was basically like going to a stripped down, on-campus cafeteria rather than your Americana lunchrooms. 

It was definitely popular, they regularly had lines there with at least one or two people waiting, and at their most popular it was crowd-crush time, to the point where I think they may have put up that temporary railing a la cinema kiosk dividers to try and curb the crowds. Writing this, I definitely recall getting in line fairly close to end-of-lunchtime, and experiencing the bell ringing before I could get my greased treats, I can feel the disappointment part of my brain tingling in that nostalgic way.
I think we might have had an unrelated Lunch Program for less fortunate students, but I'm not sure. We may have had informal versions of that, both in secondary and primary school, because at the very least apples are cheap and delicious and *someone* will have them so why not, right?

It did provide me with one of my anchors for price comparisons. 1 Kangaroo Coin got you one decent-sized potato cake, and I gleefully parted ways with four joke dollars for a luxuriously greasy sheaf of potato. Now I shake my head at fish-and-chip places that sell these for $1.50 (though not with much seriousness. I tell you what, though, one of our supermarkets used to sell this box of pantry cookies, really good buttery and not-that-crumbly cookies, for 4 KCs, and then bumped that price up to *6*, with a "Always Special" or whatever label they use to make you think there's a sale on when nothing could be further from the truth, I genuinely felt like causing a scene when I found this out. They were good cookies).

Adding ketchup according to local lengend (for a very long time Heinz owned the trademark/right to use the K, making C for all other versions) was considered low brow and only 'sloppy joes' would eat it.

Author: @AldoSchmedack
Content: I am in Iowa and yes it came from Iowa. No bias. Maidrites are a chain here of loose beef sandwiches (no tomatoes, just loose beef). Both them and sloppy joes come from great depression era or even a hair before. We all use ketchup here as base as well, just like usda recipie. Cooked in large crockpots even in schools.  I did 2 years food service at a school. My guess is someone added the ketchup when cooking to try it and ended up liking it as it concentrates the tomato flavor. Add ins are garlic, garlic powder, a little mustard, onions (white or yellow), or a little worctershire sauce. A food I never get tired of. I suspect it got started up in Woden/Britt/Titonka IA area where the hobos have the national convention. It is an old depression era dish here for sure. Cuba I doubt had ketchup in 30's to make it.

Content:
If the US military had Sloppy Joes, the Korean military had what we call "red meat." 
It was literally meat cooked in red oil and sauce. It was usually pork and gochujang and gochu oil, and if you were a Korean born male and you were in an area that wasn't directly supported by the capital city government, like the Capital Defense Force, it was a dish you would see quite often. 
Not bad, but that's enough food to get you out of that shithole if you see it often enough for 3 meals 5 days out of 7(and 2 freaking years stright), in other words, the problem is that since most of the food procurement in the Korean military is a system that relies on support from local companies or large corporations, the food they give you is practically all the food you will see on a daily basis in the military.

Author: @sarahgould5435
Content: My favorite take on Sloppy Joe's was a recipe my Dad made from scratch out of his own head. My Dad was temporarily working from home and my Mom went to work in a local factory, so for the first time ever, my Dad was serving us dinner. I was 8 and, up until then, we didn't even know Dad *could* cook. I was actually expecting cold cut sandwiches for supper, so when Dad started getting the skillet out, we all asked him what he was making. He told us it was "Dad's Country Barbecue." Alas! That recipe is now lost to time, because the secret essential ingredient was 1/2 capsule of cayenne. Supplement shelves no longer offer cayenne as a rule, certainly not in the mini-ampoule collagen capsules. Since we never figure out how much of a teaspoon was contained in half a capsule, there's no way to get the proportions perfect anymore.

Author: @chrisleblanc581
Content: I was very lucky. Chef tuned stay at home mom was unhappy with the food being served to the neighborhood elementary school her children attended. Principle said you want better, come work for me. She did. I did not realize how bad cafeteria food was until I started middle. We had fresh baked bread every day. Not the typical American fluff stuff. A nice heavy bread. The whole school smelled of it until lunch. She also was a pioneer of the school yard garden trend in a way. A few classes each week south be bussed to near by farms for lessons on food cycle and a contest on which class could pick the most seasonal veg (corn, green beans, purple hull peas, butter beans, merliton/ chayote, squash, leafy green) with the winner getting ice cream or frozen cokes on Friday).  It added a lot of very high quality fresh veg to the menus. I learned to love veg. Greens with ham ant pot juices over fresh corn bread. Yum. We did all kinds of crazy stuff. Oh, a fav was when they broke out 60 ice cream makers (old crank kind) and classes competed on getting it to set, and getting it packaged into single serve bags and in an ice chest with dry ice. Our food was fantastic. Breakfast and lunch tasty and cheap. No one brought lunches. Then I started middle school and nearly puked at the first lunch I ate.

Author: @porkrind
Content:
Asked Chatgpt to explain catsup vs. ketchup: Alright — imagine Max Miller from Tasting History explaining it.
Here’s how he’d break it down, in his classic excited but precise style:


---

[Max, smiling wide, holding a little bottle]
"Today we're talking about ketchup — or is it catsup? Well, both are actually correct... sort of. Let’s go back a few centuries, because of course it has a fascinating history.

The word ketchup comes from the Hokkien Chinese word kê-tsiap, which was a kind of fermented fish sauce. Traders picked it up in Southeast Asia in the 17th century and brought it to Europe — but here’s the thing: they didn’t bring the actual sauce, just the idea of it. Europeans tried to recreate it using ingredients they had, which eventually led to all sorts of weird early ketchup recipes: mushroom ketchup, walnut ketchup, anchovy ketchup... very little tomato involved.

Now, spelling? Oh, spelling was just a suggestion back then. Some English speakers called it catchup, others catsup, and eventually ketchup. All of them were floating around in the 18th and 19th centuries. Catsup especially got popular in parts of America.

But! In 1876, Heinz — yes, that Heinz — decided to call their new tomato-based version ketchup, and thanks to their massive success, ketchup became the dominant spelling pretty much everywhere.

So while catsup isn’t technically wrong, it’s a bit like calling a television a 'talking picture box' — people know what you mean, but you’ll sound like you’re from a history book.
And if you call it catchup? Honestly, you might just need some ketchup to eat your words."

Author: @taint_misbehavin
Content: If you want a different take on a sloppy joe, skip the sauces, liquids & spices, and add diced bell pepper and jalapeno (and more onion! thinly sliced will reduce faster later). Season the meat (salt & pepper), then fry, making sure the meat gets the maillard reaction browning for more flavor. Then remove the meat but keep the fat in the pan. Use the fat to cook the onions, bell peppers and jalapenos down (add more fat if there's not enough to fry with; olive oil goes well) until they are well reduced, about 30 minutes. Then add the meat back, stir and cover, simmering for 15 minutes. Add salt & pepper to taste. You can serve it as a sloppy joe, or mix in some gochujang and use as a Bibimbap topping.

Author: @longroth4882
Content:
Growing up in the 50's & 60's my grandma would make her version. Hers didn't use any vinegar or brown sugar that many associate with it, when she made it with all that it wasn't Sloppy Joe, it was BBQ. Her Sloppy Joe was so simple, season with salt & pepper and brown ground beef with diced onions and green peppers, drain grease, add ketchup, water, mix and reduce. the ketchup will turn to a paste that sticks to the meat, and adds a great flavor. I still make them that way for gatherings, and they're always a hit. I grew up in a frugal household, so the fewer ingredients the better.

Her loose meat was just browned ground beef with larger diced onions, salt & pepper with american cheese mixed in with it, the sandwich was served on toasted bread with more cheese.  Still make those too 😋

Author: @andreagelenter
Content:
Sloppy Joes were the highlight of school lunch waaaaay back in the time machine. I was in elementary school in the '70's. They were also the highlight of summer camp lunches, with grilled cheeses coming in at a very close second place. I have no recollection of what was served with them at school other than the little carton of milk. My mom made them at home occasionally, and always served them with pineapple tidbits (do they even sell those anymore?) and potato chips, which she only bought to go with Sloppy Joes.
I have another fond memory of eating Pizza Burgers, which were made with those "gourmet" hamburger buns the Sloppy Joes were served on. The buns were opened up, some of the wonderful tomato sauce only found in school cafeterias spread on them, a slice of Govt. Issued American cheese slapped on top of that, and under the broiler until the cheese melted. I remember impressing my grandmother by making pizza burgers for her for lunch when I was in 4th grade. Thanks for the memories!

The cooking method "ground beef broken up in water, about a 1/4 inch of the pan filled with water (with the beef), then cooked until most of the water reduces, salt to taste". Throw that on a non toasted bun with diced onion, mustard, and pickle. It's great. The water reduction keeps the beef flavor but adds moisture. Don't forget to serve it with a spoon to pick up the lost crumbles. It's great. You should do a video on loose meat sandwiches.

Author: @matthewmarin703
Content: Have a look at the book "Potions Of The Caribbean" by Jeff Berry. Sloppy Joe's was a bit of a phenomenon in the day, producing their own brand of rum, cigars, and other goods that sold quite well, as did anything else with the name on it. Their sandwich menu included, among other things, a sandwich that matched the description of the ham-tongue-coleslaw concoction that you described, which probably served as the taproot for the modern "New Jersey Sloppy Joe". They also offered a sandwich that was essentially a scoop of ropa vieja stuffed into a roll, and that's where I think what most of us think of today as a Sloppy Joe comes from; once it made its way back to the states, cooks started swapping out the strips of beefsteak for more economical and quicker-cooking ground beef, and dropped the strips of pepper and whatnot in favor of shelf-stable dried spices and canned sauces for seasoning.

Content: I subscribed on titanic month. This show is a legitimately great show. I have a distinct memory of my Australian mother answering, "What's for dinner, Mum?" with, "Its this incredible new dinner I just found out about. Sloppy Joe!" But going through this episode, Mum actually had the right spirit all along. It was just a slop it together on some heat, add a little vinegary sweetness with tomato in it and then toss it in a bun kind of meal. Good memory dive on this. So… I made the recipe.  *My advice:  If you currently have a sloppy Joe recipe you enjoy - stick with it.*  

While these are ‘edible’, they’re not ‘enjoyable’.  They just don’t have much flavor to them compared to other recipes I’ve tried for the same thing.  It’s what you’d expect from government food. 😁 

There may be some people who prefer not to have a lot of flavor in their meals, and that’s perfectly fine; but in our house we want to enjoy what we’re eating and not just _’eat to survive._ 

While I was a kid in the 80s/90s school system, I don’t remember our sloppy joes being this bland.  I asked my husband, who was also an 80s kid, and he said he didn’t either.  We’re both certain that the ‘lunch ladies’ added their own flair to the recipes and they made them taste better. 


_To wit:  My background includes culinary arts history and education, I am not a ‘novice cook.’  The recipe was followed precisely, because we wanted that nostalgic experience.  Sadly, it disappointed us._

Author: @roecocoa
Content:
Because I like math and pain, I tried to work out the proportions for an 8-serving recipe.

• 22 ounces (625 grams) ground beef
• 1.5 ounces (40 grams) minced *mature* onion
•    -or- the faintest whisper of dehydrated onions
• a pinch (2 grams) of garlic powder
• 4.5 oz. (128 grams) tomato paste
• 4.6 oz. (130 grams) ketchup/catsup
• A bit less than a cup (about 210 ml) water
• A dash (4.5 grams) dry mustard
• Just a hint of black pepper
• 1 tbsp (14 grams) brown sugar, packed

I can see where the 50- and 100-serving recipes were extrapolated from an 8-serving recipe. With the dry ingredients, converting imperial volume to metric weight is always iffy; the mustard, garlic powder, pepper, and dehydrated onions should just be "to taste" but I did my best to be precise.

Author: @room34
Content: Having grown up in Austin, Minnesota — "basically Iowa" — in the '80s, I'm very familiar with Maid-Rite, or our local variant, the "world-famous" Tendermaid. Honestly I don't think anyone in Minnesota _or_ Iowa actually calls them "loose meat sandwiches" because, yuck. In Austin we just called them "Tendermaids" and I think in places where there's a Maid-Rite shop, they call them "Maid-Rites." Anyway… they're very good. I actually prefer them over sloppy joes because I'm not always a huge fan of the sloppy joe sauce, plus with a "Tendermaid" you can get it with whatever toppings you want — cheese, ketchup, mustard, diced onion, pickles. They use a wide spatula to slather the condiments on the bun, and they actually put the slice of cheese into the big trough of "loose meat" to melt a bit before they scoop it out to put on your sandwich. Yeah… maybe don't think too much about what's in the trough, or exactly how long it's been there, or whether it's being kept at a safe temperature. All I know is it's delicious.

Author: @Stacy_Smith
Content:
Swap "brown & drain" for "90% lean, DO NOT DRAIN".

Do this for ALL recipes calling for higher fat brown & drain.

You're not losing or gaining any fat content in the final product because draining doesn't get rid of all the grease. It does, however, discard flavor.

Not draining 90% retains all the flavor, but since you're starting with a leaner blend of ground beef, you're not adding any fat. Due to the fact you're not draining it, you're subtracting any fat either.

By following this method, what you're left with a final product that contains roughly the same fat content but with a slightly more pronounced beef flavor.

I grew up in the 50's, and vividly remember my 1st grade teacher (Mrs. Ritz) asking me why I wouldn't eat the cafeteria Sloppy Joes. 
"It looks weird."
"Don't you like hamburger?"
"Yeah..."
"Ketchup and mustard?"
"Yeah..."
"Onions?"
"Yeah.."
"Well, THAT'S a Sloppy Joe! Give it a try"
I waited until she walked away. Then I took a bite...Heaven!
And I've used her diagnostic flavor forecasting method ever since!
But, please, Max. NEVER make Tuna Tetrazzini.

I have even fonder memories of the cherry cobbler but then, I grew up in Michigan and they had a good supply of great cherries back in the day. Not sure if cherry cobblers were a thing in every state or if they would taste as good as our cherry cobbler.

Kresge's snack bar had a pretty good sloppy joe as well - of which I ate much when I worked as a cashier for them 1970-73. And the Kresge/KMart apple dumplings... to die for!

Author: @adreabrooks11
Content:
Hehe!  Watching that nostalgic giggle as you taste-tested this one was a delight!  ^_^
Canadian here, in my 40s.  When I was a child, I vaguely remember an elderly relative (I think it was my great aunt) telling me that "Sloppy Joe" was a wartime term.  Propaganda art used to hype the "G.I." image - a well put-together, tidy and frugal wartime lad of good physique and excellent grooming.  A "Sloppy Joe" was sort of the opposite of this - a slumpy, inattentive guy with poor bearing and untidy ways.  I don't think it was a deliberate "character" used in wartime ads; just a psychological antithesis of what a "real man" ought to be, according to the zeitgeist of the time.  Basically a "don't be that guy" archetype.
How it got from a shabby dude to an appealing name for a sandwich I don't know - but, as you touched on, it was a playful jape toward anyone (and, apparently, anything) untidy or ill-managed.

Author: @lizajoymorales248
Content: My grandfather (his name was Chalmer Miller) had a sloppy joe sandwich shop in Lima, Ohio in the late 1940's. The recipe included ground beef, finely chopped onion, tomato juice, dry breadcrumbs, ketchup and mustard, salt and pepper. The meat, along with the finely chopped onions, was browned in its own fat, the tomato juice was then added, and it was all cooked down until the sauce was concentrated and thick. Then the ketchup and mustard were added, and next dry bread crumbs were stirred in and the pot was set aside for a half hour or so for the crumbs to absord the sauce, thickening the mixture. Finally, salt and pepper were added to taste.  More than 75 years later, his granddaughter and great-grandchildren -- now living in Spain -- are still enjoying his recipe, and it has been served to friends and neighbors here and enjoyed by all. Love ya always, Grandpa. Edit: I've been saying it is Grandpa's recipe but, after thinking it over, I believe it was probably my Grandma's recipe. I don't remember Grandpa ever cooking anything and the only time I saw him step into the kitchen was to ask Grandma (Rose Miller née Gwinner) if the upcoming meal (breakfast, lunch or dinner) was ready. Grandma, on the other hand, had been Head Cook at a TB hospital before getting married (working her way up from tray girl) and could make a feast out of practically anything. So, here's to Grandma, the best home cook ever.

Author: @brianjones6210
Content:
I still make Sloppy Joe's. I'm not sure where I got the recipe, probably from my mother in law because it is hand-written. My mother was a lunch lady, she probably used the USDA recipe, but I don't, it's too fussy.

My wife is a librarian. After the school pizza video, she got me the USDA recipe book from the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center, which is cool, because I grew up a few minutes from there and used to hang out with the cows with holes in their sides they used to study interesting things like cow digestion. There wasn't much security or adult supervision in the 1970's and '80's. Kids could just run around and do stuff.

Oh, and the government-sanctioned marijuana fields. I may have had neighbors who brought their work home with them. Let's just say that their backyard had some interesting flora.

1 lb ground beef (or turkey, I actually prefer turkey, but if you like the fat, go for it, but drain it before adding the sauteed onions)
1 tablespoon oil or butter to saute the onions
1/2 cup chopped onion
1/2 cup green pepper (optional, I don't use it)
1/2 teaspoon salt
pepper to taste
2 teaspoons Worcestershire sauce
1 cup ketchup (Heinz, there can be only one)
1/2 cup water
Cheese (I prefer white American) and hamburger buns

Brown the meat, saute the onions, combine and add everything else and simmer until it reaches your preferred consistency. Put it on a bun with cheese. Or put it on french fries.

Author: @gcvrsa
Content: As a German American descended from a family from Hamburg, Germany, I can tell you that the closest thing in traditional German cuisine to what we Americans call a "Hamburger" is what the German call "Frikadelle" or "Frikadellen" in the plural. This is really more of a flat meatball, made of whatever combination of beef and pork you prefer, often eaten cold, but put it between two slices of bread for a picnic, and you can see the similarity to the American "Hamburger". So, my guess is that anyone in Iowa making a "Hamburg sandwich" in the 1930s or 1940s would have essentially been making German Frikadellen, and serving them with bread as a sandwich, not a "loose meat sandwich". I would venture to guess that once the war started, they decided that maybe selling German food wasn't a smart marketing move.

Author: @jacquelyns9709
Content:
I used to make sloppy joes quite often. They were much more complicated than these school lunch ones. 
I put lots of chopped onion in, at least a whole large onion.  If I didn't have fresh onion,  I would put several tablespoons of dried onion in, either chopped or diced. Sometimes, I would use dried roasted onion flakes. I also added lots of garlic and bell pepper. Many times, I added the dried versions. The benefit of using dried ingredients is that they soak up the fat and juices from the meat, so there's no need to drain it. 
For the sauce, I would put in a half bottle of chili sauce, some worcestersire souce, A-1 sauce, a few drops of hot sauce, and sometimes small amounts of soy sauce, teriyaki sauce, fish sauce, or oyster sauce. I didnt put in mustard or tomato paste.
If I didn't have buns available,  I would serve the meat mixture over pasta or rice.

Content:
According to what I can find, Sandler did the SNL skit in 1994.  I graduated High School in '89 and was in college in '94 so that song/skit was well after my time eating in public school cafeterias.  I don't remember having Sloppy Joe in High School but do remember the rectangular pizza - which many of us enjoyed with a packet or two of yellow mustard squeezed on top (and which was eventually usurped by an inferior octagonal pizza - but, hey, it was still pizza and I was a High Schooler).

I do seem to remember the occasional Sloppy Joe from Middle School although just straight up hamburgers were more common.  Elementary School was a looonnnggg time ago - I started Kindergarten in 1976 - so, although I remember that the lunch ladies were very nice, kind and good cooks I don't specifically recall Sloppy Joes.

That said, Sloppy Joes were a fairly common dinner at home, especially during periods when my mom was working and we got home from school around the time she got home from work.  They were usually Manwich.

Content:
Catsup/Ketchup History
Catsup is an old term used for ketchup or more importantly tomato ketchup. Ketchup/catsup was an old Chinese mix sauce made from things like fish, shellfish like oysters and sometimes mixed with powdered mushrooms. The original Chinese name for it sounded like catsup. Later recipes for it as it spread across Europe and Britain included the famous tomato ketchup we enjoy to this day

Then mix in some amount of ketchup and yellow mustard. Just enough to hold the meat together a bit on the bun later. Simmer for a short amount of time. The official Maid-Rite served at the restaurants of that name were just the browned meat, no sauce. School Sloppy Joes had too much sauce. Homecooked maidrites were somewhere in between.

Content: I never liked any other Sloppy Joe's but my mom's. I didn't like the schools I didn't like Manwich, didn't like the ones served at others houses. So anyway, I move out and I'm trying to make Sloppy Joe's, I'm guessing 1983 for the new fiancé and they taste just like every other recipe except my mom's.  Now my mom wasn't a gourmet cook, but she fed her family, and these are AWESOME. I called her for the recipe, and she was so tickled to be asked, I mean I was her oldest child calling and asking for help at 22. I was like, why are yours so good and she said Bennetts Chili sauce.  She used two pounds ground beef, well browned and drained. (Not just no longer pink, it has to be almost fried in the beef fat) One 8 oz. can tomato sauce and one 12 oz. bottle of Bennetts Original Chili Sauce. Add water if you need to, it depends on the beef and how long you cook it after, but the meat should simmer in the sauce for 20-30 minutes, it helps tenderize it. Taste for salt? but I never do. Max, what you said about buns is so true. Nice fluffy middle class suburban white burger buns that squish a little are perfect. But, have you ever tried toasting them first, then slopping the joe on? Ambrosia. Thanks you so much for sharing. I love your channel.

Content: Well known that Hemingway was a big fan of Sloppy Joe's (the bar, not the sandwich). He enjoyed deep-sea fishing for Marlin or Swordfish, and had a an easy path from Key West (where he lived) to Havana on the same boat he fished from. There is a bar in Key West named Sloppy Joe's I visited back in '85. It is/was dedicated to all things Hemingway, with a commemorative coffee table book for a few bucks available to nerds like me (yes, I bought one). Don't know when the Key West bar opened, but it was old and probably post-21st Amendment, repealing Prohibition. I always remember Hemingway's spacious home in Key West, with its 6-toed cats. He was a fascinating human being, who was also an azzhole frequently.

Content:
Catsup! I also dislike this BUT! To get over it, I have learned how it can evolve into ketchup. Say "catsup" repeatedly, but slowly curl your tongue so it moves back along the roof of your mouth. Eventually, you'll be incapable of making an effective "s" sound and it (with the preceding t priming it) will morph into a "ch" sound. When you do this quickly (conversationally), it will happen a lot sooner, and by just repeatedly saying that at varying speeds and with varying mouth movements, you will start to get a grasp on why "catsup" became "ketchup". 

All that said? Seeing it written as "catsup" is heresy. It is insanely cursed, and I hate it with all my being. I just use this nugget of knowledge as a way to save me from disgust and rage when I encounter it.

Regarding lunch pizza, we had octagon shaped hamburger pizza.  US guys called it mirror pizza because the pizza was so greasy you could see your reflection.

Content:
I soup mine up. I mix in mustard and BBQ sauce. I also add diced and sautéed bell pepper, onion, and garlic. Also, some diced dill pickle. I prefer to add sliced olive and sauteed mushroom, but those two usually wig people out, so I omit them when I cook for others.

After that, I serve on grilled cheese melt. Sourdough bread, slice of American on one side, one slice of provolone on the other. A serving of filling on both sides (double serving makes it extra sloppy), and a slice of Swiss in the middle.

Cut into triangles and serve over a basket of crispy tater tots with your favorite hot sauce. Tater tots catch the slop, and you get loaded tots when you are done with your melt.

Content: My mother's version of Sloppy Joe's was very different. Not sure where it came from but she said this is what they had as kids. So we are looking at circa 1945-1960. So you fry 1lb ground beef in a pan, once cooked drain liquid. Add one can of Campbell's Cream of Mushroom and one dry package of Lipton's Chicken Noodle Soup. Mix through, put lid on and let simmer on low for about 10 minutes till the packaged noodles are soft. Serve on a bun. Be warned, it will be a grey looking Sloppy Joe not your traditional red. It gets mixed reviews, I would say 50% liked it and 50% did not :)

Author: @rosemaryharold8189
Content: I can tell you what a Maid Rite sandwich tasted like. I was a child in Iowa in the 1960s, and I occasionally tagged along with my dad (also an Iowa native) when he snuck out of our house on Saturdays to go to the local Maid Rite restaurant. The Maid Rite version of loose meat sandwiches were boring, at least to kids who got Sloppy Joes at school lunchtimes. The Maid Rites were just crumbled-up bits of ground beef, along with some chopped onion, salt, and pepper, I believe. They also were a mess to eat; lacking whatever adherence ketchup and/or tomato paste lent to Sloppy Joes, Maid Rite crumbled meat cascaded out of the soft bun whenever you picked up or bit into the sandwich. To boost the flavor, diners sometimes added ketchup or mustard. My dad never did, though — I guess he just enjoyed dining on his memories of the original recipe from his 1930s childhood!

Author: @Plasmastorm73
Content:
A Brief History of Ketchup and Catsup

To understand the difference between ketchup and catsup, it’s essential to examine their shared history. The origins of ketchup date back to 17th-century China, where a fermented fish sauce called “ke-tsiap” was a staple condiment. British sailors and traders brought this sauce back to Europe, where it evolved into a variety of different forms, including a sweeter, more tomato-based version.

In the United States, ketchup became a popular condiment in the late 19th century, with brands like Heinz leading the charge. However, some manufacturers began using the spelling “catsup” instead of “ketchup.” This variation was initially seen as a regional quirk, with some parts of the country preferring one spelling over the other.
Regional Preferences and Linguistic Influences

So, why did the spelling “catsup” emerge in the first place? One theory is that it was influenced by the German word “katzup,” which was used to describe a type of sauce. German immigrants brought this term with them to the United States, where it evolved into “catsup.”

Regional preferences also played a significant role in the adoption of “catsup” versus “ketchup.” In some parts of the country, particularly in the Midwest and Northeast, “catsup” was seen as the more traditional or authentic spelling. This may have been due to the influence of local manufacturers or cultural traditions.

Ground beef, sauteed onion and garlic, canned tomatoes, tomato paste, ketchup for the taco filling, then oregano, chili powder, related spices.  As an adult, sometimes I've added a splash of balsamic vinegar.  And yeah, it's hard not to just eat it all out of the saucepan.

(Also, I think my family didn't drain the fat. I certainly don't.)

Health, I dunno.  Ground beef and tomato stuff. Could be worse.  Another video about Joe's said that schools liked them because more vegetables could be snuck into them. One of the recipes you flashed past mentioned celery, maybe carrots. Dropping the cheap buns and using whole wheat bread or pasta improves the fiber levels of the meal a lot.

That military ad had me thinking "only 1/6 lb beef for an American soldier? Maybe that's the real problem."

Content:
Great video, looks like you really had fun making it.
Growing up in Scotland in the 70s, the only "Sloppy Joes" reference we had was to casual or lounging clothes. We did however have "mince rolls". Was something of a rainy Saturday afternoon treat in our house. It consisted of a by then ubiquitous in Scotland "Morton's roll" with some heated up mince plopped in it. In our house the mince would have onions & peas in it, plus a handful of oats added. This thickened it up a bit, made it go further, added fibre & slow release energy. I think most Scottish homes would have a pot of mince mouldering on the stove as it would be a common meal for at least a couple of days a week. The basic mince could be turned into mince & tatties, cottage pie, spaghetti bolognaise & in the more "adventurous" households chilli con carne or stuffed peppers. 🫑😆 So yeah I have good memories of a similar dish, reading my comic or watching an old B&W film while the rain battered the windows.

At Billy Boy in Riverside it's actually listed on the menu as "loosemeat", but elsewhere it's treated as a signature menu item. Author: @djPaigeRailstone
Content: My husband has a full beard, but I LOVE sloppy joes. To forego his suffering from the sloppiness of the sloppy joes, I would make it less sloppy. Make the meat sauce exactly as directed, then instead of placing it onto buns, cut a loaf of french bread in half and place on a baking tray. Dish the meat out onto both halves and sprinkle with a tiny bit of colby-jack cheese, then bake in the oven for 12 minutes at 375F. Slice into three inch portions. You get that sloppy joe flavor, but instead of a soggy bun you get a crispy crunch from baking, and the cheese helps the meat stay put on top.

Author: @CharlesSummers-d1v
Content:
Sloppy Joes are a “guys” meal made in heaven!!! 
😀
At age 67, I love them and make them myself about 2 to 3 times per year.
I always use 2 pounds of hamburger meat which for me, makes 4 meals…I eat 1 and put the other 3 meals in sealed, microwavable glass bowls in the fridge for the next week or so.
🙂
I must say that I use “Manwich” and for 2 pounds of meat I use 2 cans.
The Manwich also has minced, green bell pepper in it which for me are a key flavor ingredient. 
When I brown the meat I add salt & pepper and Worcestershire sauce…and sometimes some extra onion powder.
When done, I pour off as much liquid fat as possible.
Once the Manwich is added along with some warm water that I rinsed the cans out with, I also add a name brand, Sloppy Joe, powder spice package to enhance the flavor, usally French’s. 
I allow it all to simmer on low, frequently stiring so as not to burn or spatter out onto the stove top.
😀
Once done…O-M-G is it SOooooooo GOOD!
Being retired, I usually follow it up with some TV on the recliner and a nap. 
That is almost mandatory. 
😀
Great topic today…I really enjoyed it.
🙂
Sloppy Joe fan in Georgia - USA

I went to visit her up in Oregon and she said she was making Sloppy Joe's and I said, "Oh good you can teach me the recipe!" 

Because I  had become somewhat of a cook myself I was excited to learn another one of her famous recipes.  

In the words of Samuel L Jackson, "Hold onto your butts!""

 Brown the hamburger and put in equal parts, ketchup, and mustard and that was it.   

That was the ENTIRE recipe:  brown 2 pounds of hamburger and a cup of ketchup and a cup of yellow mustard, and mix it together and serve it, on a toasted bun.

Soooooooooo good!!!!It's kind of ridiculous. I had the same reaction you did in your video just now. It was exactly as I remembered it.  This was a once a week stable dinner in the summer and maybe once every two weeks in the winter depending on whether or not she had a hamburger helper box available. 

She had gotten the recipe from her mom who I'm sure learned it you know during World War II.

Content: I kinda want to believe the Cuban origin theory.  I mean, this sandwich is just picadillo in a bun, right?  Sounds like something they'd eat in Cuba, right along with their vacas fritas and medias noches.  I would imagine that the recipe for the picadillo itself may have morphed a bit to fit American ingredients and palates (I don't see Spanish olives, cumin, or raisins, for example, but those might be much newer additions to picadillo anyway), but picadillo is still ground beef in a tomato-based sauce, and that's exactly what a Sloppy Joe is.  Cubans would probably also use a different kind of bread, but again, if some American went to Cuba and had a picadillo sandwich, they could easily have come back to the US and adapted the recipe into the modern Sloppy Joe (under whatever name, I guess).

Author: @OriginalCaliKitty
Content:
Being an old person, my experience with sloppy joes was in the 50s when I was a kid and my Mom would make them for dinner. I don't know what recipe she used, but I loved them. (She once told me that she and Dad were so poor when they first got married that she learned a hundred ways to cook ground meat, which must have been cheaper than chicken then.) She didn't make them often when I was a teen, not sure why. As far as a school cafeteria version, I went to a small Catholic school in Ohio and we didn't have a cafeteria until I was in 4th grade. When we did get one I ate the food, but not for long because it was awful. The only thing I remember was the cream of tomato soup, which was the same color as Pepto-Bismol. It didn't taste like much, but if you could make someone laugh at the lunch table when they were eating it, it was pretty spectacular when it came out their nose! 

When we moved to L.A. I went to public junior high and high school (no middle school back then). I never set foot in either cafeteria - I was warned off by other kids. Fortunately, both schools had "snack shacks" to raise money. So, in junior high my friends and I usually had an ice cream bar or popsicle for lunch. The high school shack sold plate-sized cookies, so that's what my friend Jan and I usually ate; however, if we were hungrier, we'd get one of the soggy hot dogs, which came with a strange sauce that Jan decided to call "mung." (I think it was some kind of Thousand Island.) Nobody thought much about nutrition in the 50s/60s - we ate crap, drank Tang, and thought water from the backyard hose was a fine source of refreshment when playing outside. But then we also ate icicles speckled with soot, breathed polluted air (a friend once said she didn't trust air she couldn't see), and thought we'd soon be vaporized in a nuclear cloud. Fun times.

Author: @endormorre6567
Content:
I genuinely think women's Sloppy Joe fashion is one of my favorite styles, even before I realized it had a name. While I never think you should look down on any style of dress when done for your own comfort or expression, required fashion feels like such a waste of effort. Having the confidence in yourself to put your own comfort first and not caring what others think of you is extremely attractive, both platonically and romantically. 
There is also that removal of separation from who a person presents to be and who they really are. Clothes are Kool because of their ability to act as a costume, allowing you to tape into the feeling of a mind set most associated with the garment. I think Sloppy Joe's actually accomplished the same thing. The lack of care in your presentation and aim to comfort does a lot to combat the artificial social gymnastics interacting with other people society in general and a more put together style can impose.
As much as I thought my original reason for liking this kind of dress because of the simulated intimacy it creates by presenting a style you would usually only see with someone you live with, I don't think removing masks encourages more sincerity. If anything the opposite is true because when we ourselves, it's not because we stop pretending to be someone we aren't, it's when we start trying to be an us we want to become.

Content:
Since you mention Russian Dressing I have to recommend it -- I only recently realized how good it can be.

On several occasions at restaurants I was served dishes that had what I thought was Thousand Island Dressing. I was repeatedly surprised it was so tasty. Thousand Island is a kiddie dressing I long ago gave up.

If you find bottled Russian Dressing in stores, it's almost always sort of French Dressing and not interesting at all.

Suffice it to say, Russian Dressing (and Louie Dressing) are grown-up, less sweet Thousand Island. 

Chili sauce or cocktail sauce instead of plain ketchup. (You can turn ketchup into those sauces pretty easy and they're cheaper that way.) Herbs, fresh preferably, are important. Tarragon is key (Andrew Zimmern agrees with me.) Horseradish is usually an ingredient but it shouldn't be in-your-face.

Author: @mrnekrell15551
Content: One thing i always envied to the americans. Here in Italy, public school cafeteria were awful when i was a kid. I don't know if it is still so. Normaly, school cafeterias don't have a real kitchen, everything was made by a private kitchen, that could be relatively far from school. All the food was stewed, or boiled or in water bath, except some rare baked potatoes and a couple of other items. When ready the food was stored in water bath for both the transportantion and the wait before lunch. That means HOURS of water bath. Everything was always flacid, watery, barely warm and smelling of sweat. Everything was saltless, completely and the teachers didn't allow us to use any seasoning in fear of over use. Only vinegar was, not allowed, enforced if you dared to ask for it. They would make your food float in vinegar if you lamented of its taste. Pasta with tomato sauce, rice with tomato sauce, the so called "sand bucket", an overly watered cornmeal polenta, soup, stew, boiled vegetables, sometimes salad, sometime 1 (ONE, thankfuly) slice of cheese plus the two "special days", our favorites: boiled potatoes and 2 (TWO) slices of ham and the """""PIZZA"""""... that was just some really tall steamed bread, again saltless and watery, with some tomato sauce and dry mozzarella melted and burned on. This absolutely ruined food for me in adulthood. I'm italian and i love cooking but i hate eating and i can't stand the smell of cheese, vinegar and boiled vegetables anymore. If i will ever have kids, they are going to have their Sloppy joe day, i swear it.

Content:
Here's my sloppy Joe recipe 
1/2 TBSP Oil
1 lb ground beef 80/20
     Start to brown halfway 
           Add
1/3 cup packed brown surgar
1-2 TBSP  Monteal Steak Seasoning
     Finish Browning
           Add
 1 Yellow Onion Chopped/Diced
 1 Red Pepper Chopped/Diced
 2 TBSP Red Wine vinegar
2 TBSP Worcestershire Sauce
    Let simmer, cover if needed
            Add
One 15oz Can Tomato Sauce
2 TBSP Tomato Paste
Simmer

Add red beans and some adobo sauce from chipotle's in adobo to make chili


Also I'll just add extra of whatever spices/other ingredients to taste if I'm looking for a stronger flavor
